review_scope: Independent first-reader readability only, for a mathematically capable high-school or college student with basic mathematics. This is not factual review or benchmark replication.
intro_summary: The appendix separates four things that can easily be confused: writing a solution, trying more answers, selecting an answer, and training from feedback. It uses small arithmetic tasks with checkable answers to compare correctness, candidate success and computing cost, then explain how feedback changes an answer probability. Its examples illustrate measurable procedures and numbers; capability still needs evaluation on new questions.
reader_summary: The question is whether making a model write intermediate steps helps it solve a problem. For 2+3, a bare 5 and counting 3,4,5 can both be right; a longer explanation provides checkable intermediate results that later generated text can use, but costs more tokens and can carry errors forward. SFT can teach either answer form, so form alone is not evidence of improved reasoning. The code supplies two human-written answers to the same question, encodes only each answer with ByteTokenizer, and prints lengths. Its short answer is one token; the long answer has five ASCII digit bytes and fourteen three-byte characters, totaling 47 tokens. It never trains or judges arithmetic. The separate cited experiment trains two small models from copied random weights on (a+b)+c, where a,b,c each take six values 0 through 5, giving 216 ordered questions. Permutations of the same numbers stay in the same family, so the held-out questions test unseen combinations within the same number range. Training/validation/final questions are 167/25/24 and families 44/6/6. Both branches use the same seed, batch size, learning rate and 900 updates; their answer forms produce different numbers of supervised token targets. At temperature 0.7 one generated candidate per final question gives 1/24 correct short answers and 11/24 correct step answers, leaving 13 step errors. NLL is the mean negative natural log of the correct next-token probability when the correct answer prefix is supplied, including EOS targets. Thus 4.3159 is already an average across the 51 short-answer final targets. The step branch uses 466,322 training targets versus 48,803, about 9.6 times as many, and has a longer generation limit. The observation supports this particular recipe, with a budget caveat; the different answer contents also prevent interpreting their NLLs as one general ability scale. I can predict the exercise: changing only the final 5 to 6 leaves 47 tokens but contradicts the earlier count. Running it confirms that length output alone misses this error.

terminology.details: After the explicitly linked prerequisites, token is a piece or structure marker handled by the model; this example uses one UTF-8 byte per token. SFT is supervised fine-tuning on answer demonstrations; EOS is an end marker that is absent from the first code example but included in the experiment target counts. Random weights are the starting adjustable numbers, seed fixes the random process, width describes internal features, layers repeat model blocks, and the two heads are parallel attention groups rather than two output heads. NLL and temperature are sufficiently explained in C.1. Two experiment-setting terms remain unglossed, learning rate and context capacity, recorded as low nonblocking issues because their equal-setting role is still clear. No undefined term blocks the lesson argument or exercise.

examples.details: I can explain why both 2+3 answers are correct, why the longer one might help later generation, and why a wrong middle result can mislead it. For the experiment, each of a,b,c has six allowed values, so 6×6×6=216; reordering one set of three numbers stays in a family, rather than becoming a training/test leak across permutations. The question counts sum to 216 and family counts to 56. a,b,c are the three addends; the parentheses fix the first addition. 64 is the shared feature width, two the layer and head counts, 128 the stated context setting, 42 the seed, 24 the training batch size and final question count, 0.003 the common learning-rate value, 900 the updates, and 0.7 the sampling temperature. The training targets 48,803/466,322 and final targets 51/510 count answer supervision including EOS, while the four NLL values are means rather than totals. 11/24 leaves 13 errors and 466,322÷48,803≈9.56 supports the approximate 9.6 factor. These are my arithmetic readings of cited numbers, not independently reproduced experiment results. The missing generation-limit values are noted without blocking the caution about unequal cost.

program_explanation.details: The sole fenced block imports ByteTokenizer, makes one tokenizer object, and builds a list of two dictionaries with the same question but different answer strings. The for loop takes each answer, encode returns its token ID list, and len counts that list; print shows the question, answer and token count. No model object, loss, update, correctness check, chat boundary or EOS is added here. I saved the exact fence and predictions before execution, then ran it in the existing .venv offline with GPU visibility disabled. Actual stdout is 2+3=? 5 回答token數 1 and 2+3=? 從2開始數三次：3、4、5，所以是5。 回答token數 47, matching my prediction. The model experiment later in the prose is a separate cited earlier run that I did not execute.

exercise.details: The instruction changes only the last digit in the second answer, giving 從2開始數三次：3、4、5，所以是6。. Before execution I predicted an unchanged 47 because the replaced ASCII digit is still one byte, while the listed count ends at 5 and disagrees with the conclusion 6. The changed script prints 47 and no error flag, exactly as predicted. Checking reasoning quality would therefore need a check of both the final arithmetic answer and the intermediate chain, rather than this length-only loop. The requested edit and check are unambiguous.
